There have been many previous attempts to characterize and dissect mechanisms of Na/K pump regulation in the heart. Most have examined a single pathway or pathway component under one or another condition. Over the years this has resulted in a confusing patchwork of loosely connected, and occasionally conflicting, findings that have offered little consistent insight. The present work raises the bar for future studies aimed at this topic by demonstrating the breadth and depth of high-resolution measurements required to draw reliable conclusions.

Here, in the course of examining the causes of Na/K pump current decline during brief periods of exposure of cardiac myocytes to pump-activating extracellular K, Hilgemann and colleagues have uncovered evidence for an inactivation process that appears to regulate the activity of Na/K pumps under roughly physiological conditions. At least as important, they provide evidence for possible modulation of that inactivation by manipulations that raise cytoplasmic Ca concentration. Shockingly, the magnitude of the modulation identifies it as probably the largest physiological regulator of cardiac Na/K pump function found to date. Moreover, the authors' exhaustive search for the underlying Ca-dependent modulatory pathway seems to have ruled out all the usual suspects, forcing them to consider effects mediated by changes in physico-chemical properties of the cell membrane itself.

The authors present a large amount of carefully controlled experimental data, obtained in intact cardiac myocytes with adequately controlled intracellular and extracellular environment and rapid external solution exchange. The data include measurements of cell membrane current and capacitance, or cytoplasmic Ca concentration. Not surprisingly, among the wealth of experimental information are findings that prompt further questions. Obvious ones are what are the origin and mechanism of the extracellular K-induced decrease in the capacitance signal, which is shown in Figure 1B to be ouabain sensitive, and which recovers relatively slowly (10s of sec) after K withdrawal with a time course that seems to mimic both recovery of Na/K pumps from inactivation and recovery of hydrophobic cation current amplitude from K-induced depression (Figure 12)? Could the capacitance signal in the absence of K include a component of charge movement within the Na-bound phosphorylated Na/K pumps that is then lost when K binds and drives the Na/K exchange evident as net outward current? (Those pump charge movements are known to be diminished at low external Na concentration, but might be evident in high-resolution measurements). Could the slow recovery of that capacitance signal reflect unbinding of the last K ion, given the pump's expected μM K affinity in the near absence of external Na, the millimolar concentration of K applied, and the possibility of diffusion-limited spaces containing high-affinity K binding sites (T-system, between sarcolemma and coverslip)? A pump origin for that capacitance component is supported by its abolition by ouabain (Figure 1B) and by its doubling when pump cycling current was similarly doubled (Figure 7). If so, the latter parallel changes in the capacitive and stationary pump current signals could imply a temporary increase in the number of functioning pumps following episodes of Ca entry. The authors acknowledge that increased membrane capacitance after Ca entry could reflect membrane fusion events, but argue that the implied overall ~2% increase in membrane area is hard to reconcile with doubling of pump currents. But if the reversibly inserted membrane were specialized – e.g. T-tubular or caveolar – perhaps this might be possible? A little further discussion of ramifications of the clearly documented capacitance signal changes would help the interested reader.

Given the complexity, variety, and sheer abundance of the data, the authors tread carefully through what could otherwise be a minefield in trying to describe them succinctly and clearly, with one exception. The very prominent shorthand phrase "calcium transients" is not clear and is not defined anywhere. Calcium transients are mentioned in the Title, Abstract, Introduction and first sentence of the Results, and the "stimulatory effects of Ca transients" are introduced in the last paragraph of the Introduction and in Figure 7, whose title attributes the stimulation to "a train of excitation-contraction coupling cycles". The text reasonably clarifies that entry of extracellular Ca via reverse Na/Ca exchange triggers a series of contractions by Ca-induced Ca release, which stops on Ca withdrawal; that text does not mention Ca transients. Nor does the next paragraph, though its title announces "Repeated Ca transients…" and it describes effects of "two consecutive Ca influx protocols" and, later, of "a second Ca influx episode". Those latter usages suggest that a Ca transient means an episode of Ca influx, whereas the previous paragraph might be read as implying that a Ca transient is a single Ca-induced Ca release event, many of which occur during a Ca influx episode. The confusion is not helped by phrases like "the first pump current transient after the Ca transient" (subsection “Stimulatory effects of Ca transients do not appear to involve classical signaling pathways”), or "effects of extended Ca transients" (subsection “Physiological regulation of cardiac Na/K pumps by Ca transients”). If the phrase "Ca transient" is retained it will be essential to define it clearly early on (e.g., transient increase of cytoplasmic Ca concentration) and then to use it consistently.

Reviewer #2:

This work describes experiments addressing inactivation of Na/K pump currents and regulation of pump activity by Ca transients in myocytes. The experiments are rigorously done, and suggest that Ca transients associated with reverse Na/Ca exchange profoundly regulate pump activity. The results do not offer a clear mechanistic explanation but nevertheless are significant because they extend established ideas about regulation of Ca(i) by Na/K pump activity and show that reciprocal regulation of exchange and pump activity occurs, and further that this regulation involves mechanisms independent of previously examined candidates like kinase activity, phospholemman, and redox changes. The authors also rigorously analyze and highlight discrepancies between data and predictions of models of inactivation due solely to ion depletion. Further, the authors use hydrophobic ions to show that changes in membrane properties accompany regulatory changes of pump activity. The strength of the work is its rigor and demonstration of a potentially quite important phenomenon in cardiac myocyte physiology, as well as in presenting some potential challenges to current ideas. Its weakness stems from the fact that the mechanisms underlying key observations remain largely obscure. Although the work may be criticized as descriptive, the phenomena are novel and will certainly stimulate further work.

1) The authors establish correlations between pump activity and capacitance, e.g. low Na(i) is required for both a capacitance decrease and for pump inactivation in response to K superfusion. The authors suggest that capacitance changes likely reflect physical changes in addition to membrane trafficking, which is an interesting idea based in part on niflumic acid and C6TPP effects on capacitance, but this mechanism and connection is unfortunately somewhat obscure. Still, an important idea raised by the work is the potential physiological significance of modulation of pump activity by Ca(i), and the existence of a potential feedback loop with linkage to capacitance/physical membrane changes. A single exchanger-mediated Ca transient induces capacitance decrease, repetitive Ca transients induce a large increase, and a single large Ca transient (using FPL64176) induces a decrease. This apparent frequency effect is not discussed; is there any potential mechanistic explanation for apparent dependence on frequency of transients versus quantity of Ca(i)? In addition, the niflumic acid-induced capacitance change after Ca transients increased, but was δ C/C changed? This is important with respect to the postulated relationship between Ca regulation and membrane changes.

2) The authors provide several strong lines of evidence that pump inactivation involves mechanism(s) in addition to Na depletion, and data support a model of selective inactivation from E1 Na-unbound states. A potentially more complex role of ATP is also suggested by some experiments, and this could be further discussed or explored. A prediction of the authors' inactivation model is borne out by experiments designed to deplete ATP and suppress the transient overshoot phase but it would seem to be informative to further test whether increasing glucose or including ATP in the pipette blocked or reduced the pump current inactivation, increased the steady-state current, or changed recovery kinetics. It would also seem worthwhile to test whether ATP affected inhibition of pump currents induced by multiple Ca transients.

3) An important argument concerning the selectivity of the pump-exchanger interaction is based on the experiment shown in Figure 13. This involves simultaneous washout of Ni and application of K, but the unblocking kinetics of the exchanger current following Ni removal are not shown (presumably this is fast, but should be shown or noted). The authors should show that are no pre steady-state Ni washout currents that may be additive or occlusive with the pump current. This would strengthen the conclusion that presence or absence of inward exchanger current does not affect the amplitude of pump current as predicted by a depletion model (instead, inhibition of pump currents is seen in the face of enhanced exchange current). The authors state there is no effect of Ni under "routine conditions", is there also no direct effect of Ni on K-induced pump currents?

Reviewer #3:

This well written manuscript presents convincing data for a novel and important form of Na/K pump regulation by Ca transients in the heart. Post Ca transient potentiation is clear, important and the data let no doubt about it. Furthermore, kinase and redox regulation seems to produce no effect on pump function or in its regulation by Ca. The effects of membrane modifiers are also important. All adds important data to controversies regarding Na/K pump regulation.

I don't think the evidence for pump inactivation in E1 without bound Na is conclusive enough, but such an inactivation is an attractive hypothesis that would have profound implications.

Given the insensitivity of the Ca effects to so many compounds, irrefutable proof of E1-inactivation should come from inside-out giant patches. This would allow perfect intracellular control eliminating assumptions of depleted volumes. Under the external conditions used here, if the pumps are inhibited in E1 when Na is not present, the rate of activation of Na/K pump current should differ if ATP is applied in the presence of 25 mM Na+i, than if Na+i is applied in the presence of 10 mM ATP. In order to facilitate occupancy of E1, even in the absence of ATP, the experiments could be performed in continuous presence of 1 mM ADP. Also, ideally, the effects of Ca should also be observed in inside out patches.

Small currents: The experiment with 40 mM Li+i may be misleading because the K0.5 for Li+i is above 40 mM (Hemsworth et al., 1997) and thus is equivalent to low Na+i. The currents at the end of the K application in the experiments where pump current was reduced by lowering the temperature are tiny (see also error bars). How well can this current be measured? Why weren't the currents reduced by reducing [K]o? To completely eliminate possible K-current contaminants, relevant when pump currents are tiny, it would have been better to use Cs+o instead of K+o, both for maximal and submaximal current activation (currents in K+o and Cs+o are identical in the absence of Na+o).

Regarding the table, which shows an outstanding amount of experiments convincingly demonstrating lack of kinase or redox modulation of Ca potentiation, a couple of observations require further discussion. First, the PLM -/- mice show that the currents in the absence of Ca transients, with 25 mM Na+i Fdecay is identical than in wild type mice with 40 mM Na+i both before and after Ca, although in 40 mM Ca there seems to be some reduction in Ipeak, while the PLM-/- mice have a 25% increase. Second, the membrane modifiers show another important observation. F decay was significantly reduced by methylene blue and Triacsin C, although the peak was reduced by 50%. Can these distinct effects of membrane modifiers and PLM -/-point to separate Ca-regulation mechanisms related to [Na]i?

The experiment in Figure 13B has rundown and a change in baseline. Decay in the first and third K-applications differ. Explanation?

results.result: Transient elevations of cytoplasmic Ca strongly regulate cardiac Na/K pumps by increasing peak pump currents and attenuating current decay, with effects larger than those of PKA or PKC activation. Peak pump currents increased on average by 54% after Ca elevation, current decay during K application decreased from 70% to 20%, and 10s currents increased three-fold, with effects reversing over 3 minutes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C5-C6, C32-C35, C107-C111, C159, C201, and C240 collectively demonstrate that transient Ca elevations profoundly enhance Na/K pump activity. The experimental data in Figures 6-10 show consistent, quantified effects with appropriate controls (blebbistatin to rule out mechanical effects) and statistical support (n=12 experiments). The magnitude of effects (54% increase in peak current, 3-fold increase in 10s current) is well-documented and reproducible.

results.result: Na/K pump currents decay rapidly when cytoplasmic Na is submaximal, and multiple lines of evidence suggest this reflects an inactivation mechanism rather than simple Na depletion. The inactivation is proposed to occur when Na binding sites are unoccupied, with recovery promoted by Na binding. A key prediction of the inactivation model was verified: application of extracellular Na under conditions promoting ADP accumulation suppresses the transient phase of pump currents.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C36-C39, C46-C47, C57, C77, C83-C85, C87, C100, and C192 present a coherent inactivation hypothesis supported by multiple experimental observations. The data show current decay occurs over 10-15s with >50% decay (C46-C47), the kinetics favor inactivation over depletion (C83-C87), and the critical prediction test with deoxyglucose/ADP (C100, C192, Figure 4C) provides strong mechanistic support. However, the authors acknowledge this does not definitively exclude Na depletion (C238), making this a well-supported but not conclusive result.

results.result: Classical signaling mechanisms including PKA and PKC activation have minimal effects on Na/K pump currents compared to Ca elevation. Isoproterenol, forskolin, and cAMP showed no significant effects, while PKC activator OAG showed only small (~25%) stimulatory effects. Results were similar in phospholemman-deficient myocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41, C101-C105, C10, C171, and C214 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5 and Table 1. The negative results for PKA activation are consistent across multiple approaches (isoproterenol, forskolin, cAMP), and the small PKC effects are quantified. The similarity of results in PLM-/- mice (C41, Table 1) strengthens the conclusion. The extensive testing documented in Table 1 (C10, C214) provides comprehensive negative evidence for classical signaling pathways.

results.result: Electrogenic signals mediated by hydrophobic ions (C6TPP and niflumic acid) increase and decrease in parallel with pump currents, suggesting that Ca elevation and Na/K pump inactivation cause opposing physical changes of the sarcolemma. C6TPP currents increased by 50% after Ca elevation and decreased by ~30% after pump inactivation, recovering with similar time courses to pump current recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C140-C143, C146, C154-C155, C216, C230, and C241 are well-supported by experimental data in Figures 10-12. The parallel changes in hydrophobic ion currents and pump currents are quantified and reproducible. The use of both cationic (C6TPP) and anionic (niflumic acid) probes strengthens the conclusion that membrane physical properties are changing. However, the mechanistic interpretation (C143, C216) remains somewhat speculative, as the exact nature of the membrane changes is not fully characterized.

results.result: Repeated Ca elevations suppress both Na/K pump and Na/Ca exchange currents, often accompanied by declining membrane capacitance indicative of massive endocytosis. After three or more Ca elevations, both transporter currents often became negligible.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C135-C136, C142, and C224 are supported by experimental data in Figures 8C and 10A. The parallel suppression of both pump and exchange currents is documented, and the capacitance changes provide mechanistic insight. However, the variability in these effects ("often" became negligible, "infrequently after the second repetition") suggests some experimental inconsistency. The mechanism remains incompletely understood, though the authors speculate about possible causes (C175-C177).

results.result: Na/K pump activity shows steep dependence on cytoplasmic Na with Hill coefficients >2 in the presence of cytoplasmic K. At 37°C with 90 mM K, K50 for peak current is 19 mM Na (Hill coefficient 2.4), while at 23°C without K, K50 is 4.1 mM (Hill coefficient 1.7). Temperature and K presence significantly affect pump kinetics, but fractional current decay remains similar.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64, C66-C68, C71-C74, and C161 present detailed kinetic characterization supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3. The Hill coefficients and K50 values are determined from dose-response curves with appropriate fitting. The comparison across temperatures and K concentrations is systematic. The steep Na dependence (Hill coefficient >2) is physiologically significant for the pump's regulatory role (C162-C163).

results.result: Maximal Na/K pump currents are at least 5 pA/pF when pumps are maximally activated by 110 mM cytoplasmic Na and 7 mM extracellular K, activating within solution switch times (~100 ms). Currents are effectively inhibited by 0.3 mM ouabain, and transient capacitive signals are ablated by ouabain, confirming they arise from Na/K pumps.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45, C50-C51 establish basic experimental parameters and validate that measured currents are indeed Na/K pump currents. The ouabain sensitivity (C50-C51) is critical for confirming pump identity, supported by appropriate citation (Herzig and Mohr, 1984). The capacitance changes being ouabain-sensitive (C51) provides important mechanistic information linking capacitance signals to pump conformational changes.

results.result: Extracellular Na (5 mM) suppresses pump activity supported by contaminating K in nominally K-free solutions, with a half-maximal concentration of 2.3 ± 0.3 mM. The activation of pump currents with increasing extracellular Na can be accounted for by Na competition with contaminating K, rescuing pumps from steady-state inactivation.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C96 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4A-B. The Kd determination (C92) is quantified from dose-response experiments (n=6). The TEA experiments (C93-C94) provide additional mechanistic insight. The interpretation that Na rescues pumps from inactivation caused by contaminating K (C96) is logical and consistent with the inactivation model, though it relies on the assumption that contaminating K is present.

results.result: In NCX1-overexpressing myocytes, Na/Ca exchange currents can be many times larger than pump currents (>20 pA/pF peak, 430 pA maintained after 20s), yet Ca elevations still double peak pump currents. This makes it difficult to explain current patterns in terms of a restricted subsarcolemmal Na space shared by pumps and exchangers.
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C124 present a critical test of the Na depletion hypothesis using NCX1-overexpressing myocytes (Figure 7). The large exchange currents (C118-C119) are well-documented, and the calculation that maintained currents approximate maximal Na flux (C120) is quantitatively sound. The continued pump activation despite massive Na influx (C122-C123) strongly challenges the shared restricted space model (C124), though it doesn't definitively exclude all versions of the depletion hypothesis.

results.result: During Ca elevation protocols, Fluo4 fluorescence measurements show that free Ca rises to 2.7 μM (calculated with Kd 300 nM), decays with a time constant of ~15s, and returns nearly to baseline within 15-30s. Ca changes can be reproduced with good precision after 3 minutes.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C130 provide important quantification of Ca transients using Fluo4 imaging (Figure 8A). The fluorescence increase (3.7-fold, n=7) is well-documented, and the calculation of free Ca (C126) uses appropriate parameters. The time course measurements (C127, C130) are consistent with the observed pump current changes. The reproducibility after 3 min (C128) is important for validating the experimental protocol. However, the authors note some experimental differences (solution changes not as abrupt, less vigorous contraction) that may affect quantitative interpretation.

results.result: Na/Ca exchange current shows time-dependent activation on first Ca application (corresponding to regulatory activation as cytoplasmic Ca rises), but activates immediately and to higher magnitude on second application. Pump currents are increased beyond their peak after the first Ca elevation following a second Ca elevation, indicating both transporters become facilitated.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C134 and C223 describe the facilitation of both Na/K pumps and Na/Ca exchangers by Ca elevation (Figure 8B). The time-dependent activation on first application (C131) is explained by established NCX1 regulatory mechanisms (C132, citation to Matsuoka et al., 1993). The immediate activation on second application (C133) and further pump enhancement (C134) suggest persistent regulatory changes. The parallel facilitation of both transporters (C223) is well-documented and suggests common regulatory mechanisms.

results.result: Ca influx through Ca channels (using FPL64176 to lock L-type channels open) can activate Na/K pump currents at physiological cytoplasmic Na concentration (10 mM), with both peak and 15s currents increased by >50%. Cytoplasmic K can be replaced by cesium in the protocol.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C139 demonstrate that Ca elevation effects are not specific to reverse Na/Ca exchange (Figure 9). The use of Ca channel agonist FPL64176 provides an alternative Ca influx pathway, and the results (>50% increase in pump currents, n=5) are consistent with reverse NCX experiments. The ability to use cesium instead of K (C138) is a useful technical observation. This result strengthens the conclusion that Ca elevation per se, rather than the specific Ca influx mechanism, regulates pump activity.

results.result: Outward Na/Ca exchange current is suppressed immediately after Na/K pump activity and recovers with a time course similar to pump current recovery. Exchange currents decreased by a fractional amount about one-half of the fractional decay of pump current, with an apparent Na depletion volume of 2.2 ± 0.5 pL (n=9).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81, C180, and C225 document the parallel suppression of Na/Ca exchange and Na/K pump currents (Figure 13A). The quantification of exchange current suppression (C80) and apparent volume calculation (C81) are appropriate. The authors acknowledge this is "a very persuasive argument for Na depletion" (C180) while also noting their work "suggests a plausible alternative" involving membrane changes. The parallel changes could reflect either shared Na depletion or coordinated regulation through membrane physical properties.

results.result: Large, continuous Na influx via forward Na/Ca exchange fails to enhance pump currents, although pump operation can depress reverse exchange currents.
results.evaluation: Claim C193 presents a critical test of the Na depletion hypothesis (Figure 13B). If pumps and exchangers share a restricted Na space, continuous Na influx via forward exchange should enhance pump currents, but this is not observed. The experimental design is appropriate with Ni to control exchange activity. However, the result shows peak currents were "significantly smaller" in the presence of Na influx, which seems contradictory to the claim that influx "fails to enhance" currents. The simulation in Figure 13C supports that the depletion model predicts enhancement that is not observed.

results.result: With 10 mM deoxyglucose in the pipette, pump currents ran down completely over 10 minutes, with fractional decay increasing as currents decreased. Inward HTPP currents decreased in parallel (69% decrease). The run-down is likely caused by rapid phosphorylation of deoxyglucose by hexokinases at the expense of ATP, and membrane changes appear caused by ATP/ADP changes affecting proteins that influence the bilayer.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C153 and C200 document metabolic stress effects on pump function (Figure 11). The deoxyglucose-induced run-down is well-documented, and the control experiments with glucose-6-phosphate and deoxyglucose-6-phosphate (C148) appropriately identify hexokinase activity as the cause (C149). The parallel decrease in HTPP currents (C150-C151) supports membrane involvement. However, the mechanistic interpretation (C153) that ATP/ADP changes affect proteins that influence the bilayer is speculative, though reasonable given the data.

results.result: Membrane capacitance decreases by 0.5-1% upon K application and returns slowly after K removal with a time course mimicking pump current recovery. When cytoplasmic Na is high, capacitance returns immediately, but when Na is submaximal, capacitance does not immediately return to baseline. This suggests pumps may become locked into states that cannot cycle during current decay.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49, C55-C56, C187-C188 document capacitance changes associated with pump activity (Figures 2A-B, multiple other figures). The immediate return with high Na (C55) versus slow return with submaximal Na (C56) is a key observation supporting the inactivation model. The inference that pumps become "locked into states that cannot cycle" (C57, C188) is reasonable but not definitively proven. The capacitance changes could reflect conformational changes, but alternative explanations (e.g., membrane composition changes) are not fully excluded.

results.result: Membrane capacitance routinely increased by 3-6% during 15-40s after Ca elevation, indicating membrane fusion events and/or membrane thinning. Since maximal pump currents are not increased by Ca elevation, insertion of pumps is not a viable explanation, though Ca-dependent fusion could bring proteins that mediate pump activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C106, C227-C229 document capacitance increases after Ca elevation (Figures 6, 9, 10). The magnitude (3-6%) is consistent across experiments. The inference that this reflects fusion and/or thinning (C227) is reasonable but not definitively proven. The logic that pump insertion is excluded because maximal currents don't increase (C228) is sound, assuming maximal currents were properly measured. The speculation about fusion bringing regulatory proteins (C229) is plausible but unsupported by direct evidence.

results.result: Values obtained for the cytoplasmic Na mixing volume are about 10% of expected cytoplasmic volumes of murine myocytes (~2-3 pL vs expected ~20-30 pL), with apparent exchange times of 2-3 seconds.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 present calculations of apparent restricted volume based on current decay kinetics. The calculation methodology is described in Figure 3A and appears sound. The small volume (~10% of total) and slow exchange times (2-3s) are consistent with a restricted space model. However, the authors present multiple lines of evidence questioning whether this truly represents Na depletion versus inactivation kinetics. The calculation is valid given the assumptions, but the interpretation is contested.

results.result: Na/K pumps are present at high density in mouse sarcolemma (>2000 per μm²), constituting 3-5% of membrane surface area. It is plausible that pump conformational state could influence bulk physical properties of sarcolemma, particularly if pumps are interconnected by cytoskeleton.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C158 present calculations of pump density based on maximal currents and known transport rates. The calculation (C156) uses appropriate parameters with citation support (Gadsby and Nakao, 1989). The inference that pumps constitute 3-5% of membrane area (C157) follows logically from the density and assumed pump diameter. The speculation that this high density could allow pumps to influence bulk membrane properties (C158) is plausible but remains speculative without direct evidence.

results.result: Niflumic acid (NFA) causes 1-3% capacitance increase at 100 μM, and this capacitive binding signal nearly doubled after transient Ca elevations that caused doubling of pump currents and 5% capacitance increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C145 document NFA binding changes after Ca elevation (Figure 10B). The use of an anionic probe (NFA) in addition to the cationic probe (C6TPP) strengthens the conclusion that membrane disorder, rather than electrostatic changes, is occurring (C146). The quantification (80% increase in NFA signal vs only 3-8% capacitance increase) supports the membrane disorder interpretation. However, n=5 is relatively small for this type of measurement.

results.result: At 23°C, pump currents are at least 4-times smaller than at 37°C, but fractional current decay occurs to the same extent at both temperatures (0.67 vs 0.65).
results.evaluation: Claims C65 and C189 present temperature-dependence data (Figures 2E, 3). The similar fractional decay despite 4-fold difference in current magnitude is inconsistent with a simple depletion model (where slower currents should cause less depletion) and supports the inactivation model. The data are clearly presented in Figure 3C. This is an important control experiment that helps distinguish between models.

results.result: With 40 mM Li as a Na surrogate, small pump currents (<0.5 pA/pF) could be activated, but showed unusually strong decay (>90%) despite small magnitude, consistent with the inactivation model where more binding sites are empty with a low-affinity ligand.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 and C191 present Li substitution experiments (Figure 3C). The strong decay despite small currents is paradoxical for a depletion model but consistent with inactivation. The interpretation (C77) that low-affinity ligands promote inactivation by leaving more sites empty is logical. However, Li transport by Na/K pumps is complex, and alternative explanations (e.g., Li affecting pump conformational equilibria differently than Na) are not fully excluded.

results.result: The initial rate of pump current decay increased as cytoplasmic Na decreased from 0.06 s⁻¹ at 40 mM Na to 0.14 s⁻¹ at 2.5 mM Na at 23°C. Previous work showed the rate constant increases with Na up to 100 mM with nearly the same Na dependence as pump current itself, which is inconsistent with Na depletion but supports inactivation where Na binding promotes recovery.
results.evaluation: Claims C86, C82, and C195 present kinetic arguments favoring inactivation over depletion. The cited result from Verdonck et al. (C82, C195) that decay rate increases rather than decreases at high Na is a strong argument against depletion. The authors' own data (C86) showing faster decay at lower Na is consistent with inactivation from incompletely occupied states (C87). However, the authors note their kinetic results are "somewhat more complex" than the cited work, suggesting some uncertainty.

results.result: Under conditions promoting cytoplasmic ADP generation (10 mM deoxyglucose), pump inactivation can be strongly promoted by extracellular Na. After 30s application of 120 mM Na, peak pump currents decreased to nearly their 15s value, as expected if inactivation occurred in the presence of extracellular Na.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 present a critical test of the inactivation model (Figure 4C). The prediction that extracellular Na can promote inactivation when reverse reactions are allowed (via ADP accumulation) is verified. This is stated as verifying "a key prediction of the inactivation model" (C100). The experimental design is appropriate, though the use of deoxyglucose to generate ADP is indirect. The result strongly supports the inactivation model but doesn't definitively exclude all alternative explanations.

results.result: The myosin II inhibitor blebbistatin (5 μM) blocked contractile activity but did not block the stimulatory effects of Ca elevation on pump currents, indicating effects are caused by Ca elevation per se rather than mechanical activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C113 present an important control experiment (Table 1) ruling out mechanical effects. The logic is sound: if blebbistatin blocks contraction but not pump stimulation, then contraction is not required for the effect. The data in Table 1 show similar results with and without blebbistatin. This strengthens the conclusion that Ca elevation directly regulates pumps rather than acting through mechanical stress or strain.

results.result: Results are similar in myocytes lacking phospholemman (PLM-/- mice), with Ca elevation producing similar stimulatory effects on pump currents.
results.evaluation: Claims C9 and C41 document that Ca effects occur independently of phospholemman (Table 1). This is important because phospholemman is a major proposed regulator of cardiac Na/K pumps. The data show peak currents increase from 100 to 125 (vs 154 in WT) and 10s currents from 74 to 114 (vs 111 in WT), with fractional decay decreasing from 0.26 to 0.09 (vs 0.65 to 0.28 in WT). The effects are qualitatively similar though quantitatively different, supporting the conclusion that phospholemman is not required for Ca regulation.

results.result: Experiments with high concentrations of glutathione, oxidized glutathione, superoxide dismutase, and reducing agents give no indication that redox-dependent processes are involved in Ca elevation effects. Results are similar in Peroxyredoxin6-deficient mice. Results differ from recent rabbit myocyte studies implicating glutathionylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C213, C212, C210-C211 document extensive testing of redox mechanisms (Table 1). The negative results with multiple redox modulators (C213) and in PRD6-/- mice (C212) argue against redox involvement. The authors note their mouse results differ from rabbit studies (C210-C211), with faster current decay in mice. The comprehensive negative evidence is convincing, though species differences complicate interpretation. The lack of redox involvement is surprising given the literature and warrants further investigation.

results.result: Small changes of Na/K pump activity regulate internal Ca release in cardiac myocytes via Na/Ca exchange. Na/K pumps establish Na and K gradients for ion transport and electrical signaling, accounting for a large fraction of energy expenditure, and small pump activity changes have large effects on excitation-contraction coupling.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C13-C15 present established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations (Skou 1990, Milligan and McBride 1985, Reuter et al. 2002, Hilgemann 2004). These are not new findings but provide essential context for the study. The claims are well-established in the field and appropriately cited.

results.result: Literature review of Na/K pump regulation mechanisms in cardiac myocytes, including phospholemman, PKA and PKC effects, trafficking mechanisms, and other proposed regulatory mechanisms. Results from different studies are inconsistent, with PKA activation reported to stimulate, inhibit, or have no effect on pump currents.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C30 present a comprehensive literature review with appropriate citations. The authors accurately describe the inconsistent and contradictory results in the field regarding PKA effects (C20-C24) and other regulatory mechanisms. This background establishes the rationale for their study. The claims are properly attributed to cited work and accurately represent the state of the field.

results.result: Speculation about physiological significance and future directions: Ca-dependent pump regulation may complete a negative-feedback loop in cardiac excitation-contraction coupling, may be important in skeletal muscle, and may involve physical interactions between transporters. New model systems are needed to resolve mechanistic questions.
results.evaluation: Claims C160, C162-C163, C165, C170, C215, C234-C236, C239, C242-C243 present speculation about physiological significance and mechanisms. These are reasonable hypotheses based on the data, but they are explicitly speculative ("presumably," "may," "might," "seems reasonable to suggest"). The speculation is appropriate for a Discussion section but represents future work rather than established results. The claims are clearly marked as speculation in the evidence_type.

results.result: Mechanistic understanding of Na/K pump cycle and capacitance signals: absence of extracellular K causes pumps to accumulate in E2 conformation; application of K allows cycling; Na binding to E2 configurations generates capacitive signals that dissipate during E2 to E1 transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54, C58-C59 present established mechanistic understanding of the pump cycle and capacitance signals. C52-C54 describe standard pump cycle knowledge. C58 cites the authors' previous work (Lu et al., 1995) on capacitance signals, and C59 provides experimental verification in the current study. These claims establish the mechanistic framework for interpreting the experimental observations.

results.result: With saturating cytoplasmic Na (40 mM), pump currents are not increased by Ca elevations, but the small rapid decay (19%) is fully attenuated. Peak currents decreased by 18% after Ca elevation.
results.evaluation: Claims C166, C114-C116 document that Ca effects are Na-dependent (Figure 6B). With high Na, the stimulatory effect on peak current is lost (C166, C116) but decay attenuation persists (C115). This is important for understanding the mechanism: Ca appears to affect pump Na affinity or inactivation rather than maximal activity. The data are clearly presented with appropriate statistics (n=8).

results.result: Attenuation of putative inactivation by Ca elevations duplicates the apparent increase of Na affinity ascribed to phospholemman phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claim C167 draws a parallel between Ca effects and phospholemman phosphorylation effects, both appearing to increase Na affinity. This is supported by citation (Han et al., 2010) and is consistent with the functional data showing Ca effects are most prominent at submaximal Na. However, since the authors found no role for phospholemman in Ca effects (C9, C41), the parallel may be coincidental rather than mechanistic.

results.result: Na/K pump currents can run down during whole-cell patch clamp experiments.
results.evaluation: Claim C31 is a basic observation that motivated the study. Run-down is documented in multiple figures (e.g., Figure 4C, Figure 11) and is a well-known phenomenon in patch clamp studies. This observation led to the investigation of mechanisms to reverse run-down, ultimately revealing Ca regulation.

results.result: The fundamental result is that Ca influx can strongly up-regulate cardiac Na/K pump activity by mechanisms that do not involve protein kinases or redox signaling.
results.evaluation: Claim C159 is a summary statement of the main finding, supported by the collective evidence from claims about Ca effects (C2, C5-C6, C32-C35, C107-C111) and negative results for kinases and redox mechanisms (C10, C40-C41, C101-C105, C213). This represents the core conclusion of the paper and is well-supported by the data.
